speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. To help determine the cause of your sudden vertigo, can you describe exactly what the sensation feels like—does the room seem to be spinning around you, or do you feel like you are spinning yourself?

speaker: Patient
text: 59-year-old male. The patient presents to the emergency department with a sudden-onset sensation that the room is spinning, leading to several episodes of nausea and vomiting. The symptoms started as he was going to bed and lasted for approximately 3 minutes. He mentions that he has never experienced anything like this before and currently feels at his baseline.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you. Did you experience any hearing loss, ringing in your ears (tinnitus), or a feeling of fullness in one ear during or after the episode?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Sudden-onset sensation of the room spinning. I also have Nausea, Vomiting, Dizziness.

speaker: Doctor
text: You mentioned the episode lasted about three minutes and is now resolved; does the vertigo return or worsen if you quickly look up, look down, or roll over in bed?

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: The patient is otherwise healthy with only a history of eczema. No prior episodes of similar nature. Social history: No significant social history provided.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Dix-Hallpike Maneuver: Positive, inducing nystagmus and reproducing patient’s symptoms of vertigo when head is turned to the left and laid back.

speaker: Doctor
text: The positive Dix-Hallpike maneuver on the left side strongly indicates Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV). Are you currently experiencing any other neurological symptoms, such as double vision, slurred speech, or weakness in your arms or legs?

speaker: Patient
text: Denies headaches, hearing loss, tinnitus, loss of consciousness or neurological deficits.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given the classic presentation of brief, position-triggered vertigo, a positive Dix-Hallpike maneuver on the left, and the absence of neurological or auditory symptoms, the evidence is conclusive. DIAGNOSIS READY: Left Posterior Canal Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV)
